label: hv-mol-evo-popgen
topic: Population-genetic statements usable as axioms: fixation probability, neutral substitution rate, mutation-selection balance, drift barrier, Haldane cost
summary:
Ten statements harvested and formalised; two checked against reported numbers. Only 5 of the 10 primary sources were opened (PubMed records, mostly abstracts) in the 7-minute budget; the classical formulas for the other 5 are from memory and are marked so.

Validation 1 (neutral clock, k = mu) FAILS by about 2x under naive assumptions: the pedigree mutation rate 1.20e-8 with ~35 million human-chimpanzee single-nucleotide changes gives a split of 13.0 Myr (generation 25 yr) or 15.5 Myr (29.7 yr), against fossils of 6-7 Myr. The genome length (2.8e9 bp) and generation times are my assumptions, not opened values, and ancestral polymorphism is ignored, so treat this as a real but soft failure.

Validation 2 (Haldane cost) PASSES as a consistency check: a limit of 1 selective substitution per 300 generations allows about 867 adaptive substitutions per lineage in 260,000 generations, against about 17.5 million observed, so at most ~5e-5 of them can be adaptive. The chimpanzee genome abstract independently says fixation is dominated by neutral and slightly deleterious alleles. The 300-generation figure is from memory.

Registry coverage: lean/Delphi/Kimura.lean already has neutral fixation probability (wrightFisher_fixation_one) and the neutral substitution rate (neutral_substitution_rate, _diploid, _tendsto); lean/Delphi/Favored.lean has a lower bound for favoured alleles (wrightFisherSelection_fixation_one_ge) but not Kimura's closed form or Haldane's 2s. A grep for drift barrier, mutation-selection balance, mutational/substitution load, cost of selection, nearly neutral and fixation time found only 4 hits (lean/Delphi/Genotype.lean x2, lean/assessment/inputs.json, lean/assessment/prompts/kimura-substitution-rate.md), which I did not open; no law for these exists in Kimura.lean, Favored.lean or the registry proposals (kimura-heterozygosity, maynardsmith-hitchhiking). tracks/research mentions fixation/Kimura mainly in t6-flyingfish-law.json and t2-patterns-law.json.

findings.claim: S1 Neutral fixation probability. Formal: in a Wright-Fisher population of N diploids, a new neutral mutation (1 copy of 2N) fixes with probability 1/(2N). Assumptions: neutrality, constant N, random mating. Registry: ALREADY PRESENT (lean/Delphi/Kimura.lean, wrightFisher_fixation_one, fixationProbability_eq). Falsifier: experimental-evolution barcode lineage data (e.g. Levy et al. 2015 yeast barcodes): fraction of neutral barcodes reaching fixation must equal starting frequency within binomial error.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/47.6.713 (Kimura 1962; PubMed record opened, no abstract available, formula from memory)
findings.confidence: high for the maths; source text itself not read (PubMed has no abstract)

findings.claim: S2 Fixation probability under selection (Kimura 1962). Formal: u(p) = (1 - exp(-4 Ne s p)) / (1 - exp(-4 Ne s)) for genic selection, initial frequency p; for p = 1/(2N), Ne = N, small s > 0: u ~ 2s (Haldane 1927). Assumptions: diffusion limit, additive selection, constant Ne. Registry: PARTIAL - Favored.lean proves only a lower bound (wrightFisherSelection_fixation_one_ge, fixationProbability_ge); the closed form and the 2s limit are absent. Falsifier: Lenski LTEE / barcode-lineage establishment data: establishment probability of a mutation with measured s must be within a factor ~2 of 2s.
findings.confidence: medium: formula recalled from memory; PubMed record has no abstract and full text was not opened

findings.claim: S3 Neutral substitution rate equals mutation rate. Formal: k = 2N * mu * 1/(2N) = mu per site per generation, independent of N. Assumptions: strict neutrality, constant mu. Registry: ALREADY PRESENT (Kimura.lean neutral_substitution_rate, neutral_substitution_rate_diploid, neutral_substitution_rate_tendsto; assessment prompt kimura-substitution-rate.md). Falsifier: pedigree mutation rate (trio sequencing) vs divergence/(2 x split time in generations) for a fossil-dated species pair; ratio must be ~1.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/217624a0 (Kimura 1968; PubMed record opened, no abstract)
findings.confidence: high for the statement; original text not read

findings.claim: VALIDATION 1 of S3 - FAIL (soft, ~2x). Prediction: split time T = d * g / (2 mu). Inputs: mu = 1.20e-8 (opened), ~35 million single-nucleotide changes (opened), aligned length 2.8e9 bp (ASSUMED), g = 25 or 29.7 yr (ASSUMED). Result: d = 0.0125; T = 13.0 Myr (g=25) or 15.5 Myr (g=29.7). Measured: fossils attributed to the human lineage at 6-7 Myr. Ratio 2.0-2.4. Ancestral polymorphism and a slower ancestral per-year rate are not modelled; Langergraber et al. themselves get 'at least 7-8' Myr.
findings.evidence_quote: average de novo mutation rate is 1.20 × 10(-8) per nucleotide per generation
findings.value: predicted 13.0-15.5 Myr vs fossil 6-7 Myr: FAIL by ~2x
findings.confidence: medium: two inputs (genome length, generation time) are assumptions, not opened values; the published 1.23% divergence figure could not be opened (paywall redirect)

findings.claim: S4 Haldane's cost of selection. Formal: total selective deaths per substitution C ~ -2 ln(p0) x N (about 30N for typical p0); with a tolerable selection intensity of ~0.1 per generation, adaptive substitutions occur at most ~1 per 300 generations per lineage. Assumptions: independent loci, hard selection, constant N. Registry: ABSENT (no 'cost of selection' or 'substitution load' law; Favored.lean has an expectedSubstitutions budget definition only). Falsifier: McDonald-Kreitman adaptive substitution counts (e.g. Drosophila DGRP / PopFly alpha estimates): adaptive substitutions per generation per lineage must not exceed 1/300.
findings.source: Haldane 1957, J. Genet. 55:511-524 (NOT opened; no DOI given because I could not verify one)
findings.confidence: low-medium: figures from memory, primary source not opened

findings.claim: VALIDATION 2 of S4 - PASS (consistency check). With a 6.5 Myr split and g = 25 yr (both assumed mid-values) there are 260,000 generations per lineage; Haldane's limit allows ~867 adaptive substitutions; observed ~17.5 million substitutions per lineage (half of ~35 million) = 67 per generation. So at most 5e-5 of substitutions can be adaptive; the rest must be non-selective. The genome paper's own conclusion agrees. Neutral expectation mu*L = 33.6 per generation vs 67 observed (the same 2x gap as Validation 1).
findings.evidence_quote: dominated by the fixation of neutral and slightly deleterious alleles
findings.value: Haldane max 867 adaptive vs 1.75e7 observed total; max adaptive fraction 4.95e-5: consistent
findings.confidence: medium: a consistency check, not a strict falsification test; the 300-generation limit is from memory

findings.claim: S5 Drift-barrier hypothesis. Formal: selection lowers the per-site mutation rate u until the selective advantage of a further reduction is below ~1/(2Ne) (diploid) or 1/Ne (haploid); hence across species u * Ge (Ge = coding genome size) scales negatively with Ne (log-log slope < 0). Assumptions: mutation-rate modifiers are mostly deleterious-load reducing; Ne estimated from silent diversity pi = 4 Ne u. Registry: ABSENT. Falsifier: mutation-accumulation rate table in Lynch et al. 2016 (Nat Rev Genet) supplementary: regression of log(u*Ge) on log(Ne) must have negative slope; a zero or positive slope falsifies. Note the circularity risk: Ne is derived from pi/u.
findings.evidence_quote: scales negatively with both the effective population size
findings.confidence: high that the source states this; not numerically validated here (could not open a per-species table in time)

findings.claim: S6 Drift barrier limits molecular refinement generally. Formal: a trait improvement with selective advantage s is unreachable by selection when |s| < 1/(2Ne); replication fidelity is the worked case. Assumptions as S5. Registry: ABSENT. Falsifier: same Lynch 2016 table; also error-prone polymerase fidelity vs number of nucleotides replicated per generation.
findings.evidence_quote: ultimate limits to what can be achieved set by the power of random genetic drift
findings.confidence: high for the qualitative statement; the 1/(2Ne) threshold is the standard form, not quoted from the abstract

findings.claim: S7 Mutation-selection balance. Formal: equilibrium frequency of a deleterious allele: q = mu/(h s) if partially dominant (h s >> mu); q = sqrt(mu/s) if fully recessive; for a dominant lethal, incidence at birth = 2 mu. Assumptions: infinite population, random mating, constant mu and s. Registry: ABSENT as a law (grep hits only in Genotype.lean and assessment inputs, not opened). Falsifier: gnomAD constraint table: for haploinsufficient lethal genes, summed loss-of-function allele frequency must be ~ mu_LoF/(h s); or birth incidence of a fully penetrant dominant disorder must equal 2 x per-gene mutation rate from trio data.
findings.confidence: medium: textbook result stated from memory; primary source not opened

findings.claim: S8 Haldane-Muller mutational load principle. Formal: at mutation-selection balance mean fitness is reduced by L = 1 - exp(-U) (multiplicative loci, U = genomic deleterious mutation rate per diploid genome per generation), independent of the selection coefficients. Assumptions: no epistasis, equilibrium. Registry: ABSENT. Falsifier: human trio data (Kong 2012: 1.20e-8 x 2 x 3e9 ~ 70 new mutations per birth) times the constrained fraction of the genome gives U; if U > ~2 the predicted load > 86% conflicts with observed viability unless epistasis/soft selection holds.
findings.source: Haldane 1937, Am. Nat. 71:337 (NOT opened); mutation count from https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11396
findings.confidence: medium: from memory; primary source not opened

findings.claim: S9 Nearly neutral theory (Ohta 1973). Formal: mutations with |Ne s| < ~1 behave as neutral; therefore the ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate (dN/dS) decreases as Ne increases. Assumptions: most nonsynonymous mutations are slightly deleterious; fixed DFE across species. Registry: ABSENT ('nearly neutral' not found as a law). Falsifier: cross-species dN/dS vs silent diversity pi_S (Ne proxy) in a public comparative set (e.g. Galtier 2016 PLoS Genet animal transcriptomes): Spearman correlation must be negative.
findings.source: Ohta 1973, Nature 246:96 (PubMed title search returned nothing; NOT opened). Indirect support opened: https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04072
findings.evidence_quote: dominated by the fixation of neutral and slightly deleterious alleles

findings.claim: S10 Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutation. Formal: conditional on fixation, a new neutral mutation takes on average 4 Ne generations to fix. Assumptions: diffusion limit, constant Ne. Registry: ABSENT ('fixation time' not found). Falsifier: coalescent depth in resequencing data: mean TMRCA of autosomal neutral loci must be ~4 Ne generations with Ne from pi/(4 mu); e.g. 1000 Genomes pi with trio mu.
findings.source: Kimura & Ohta 1969, Genetics 61:763 (PubMed title search returned nothing; NOT opened)
findings.confidence: medium: from memory; primary source not opened

findings.claim: S11 Paternal-age dependence breaks the constant-mu assumption behind S3. Formal: mu per generation is not constant; de novo count rises ~2 per year of father's age, so k = mu holds per generation only at fixed generation time. This is a marked assumption for any Lean statement of the molecular clock in years.
findings.evidence_quote: The effect is an increase of about two mutations per year
findings.value: +~2 mutations per paternal year; doubling every 16.5 years

key_claims: Already in the Lean registry: neutral fixation probability 1/(2N) and neutral substitution rate k = mu (lean/Delphi/Kimura.lean); a lower bound only for favoured alleles (lean/Delphi/Favored.lean).

Not in the registry as laws: Kimura's closed-form fixation probability and the 2s limit, Haldane's cost of selection, mutation-selection balance, mutational load, drift barrier, nearly neutral dN/dS-Ne relation, 4Ne fixation time.
Validation 1: k = mu with the pedigree rate predicts a human-chimpanzee split of 13.0-15.5 Myr versus fossils at 6-7 Myr - fails by about 2x under naive assumptions.

Validation 2: Haldane's limit allows ~867 adaptive substitutions per lineage versus ~17.5 million observed - consistent only if almost all substitutions are neutral, which the genome paper also concludes.
Five of ten primary sources were not opened; their formulas are from memory and flagged.

recommendations: Add Kimura's closed-form fixation probability and the 2s limit to Favored.lean; only a lower bound exists today.
Add mutation-selection balance (q = mu/(hs), sqrt(mu/s)) and the load L = 1 - e^{-U} as new registry proposals; both are short algebraic statements.
State the molecular clock law per generation, with generation time and constant mu as explicit hypotheses; Validation 1 shows the per-year reading fails by ~2x.
Before any nanopublication, open the five unopened primary sources and replace the assumed 2.8e9 bp and generation times with cited values.
For the drift barrier, pre-register the regression of log(u*Ge) on log(Ne) and address the circularity that Ne is itself computed from u.
lay_summary: Every living thing copies its DNA with small mistakes, and scientists have simple maths rules for what happens to those mistakes over time.
We collected ten of these rules, such as how likely a new mistake is to spread to everyone, and checked which ones the project has already proved by computer.

We tested one rule that says harmless changes should pile up at the same speed as mistakes happen; using real human numbers it predicted humans and chimpanzees split about 13 million years ago, but fossils say 6 to 7 million, so the simple version of the rule is off by about two times.

We tested a second rule that says helpful changes can only spread slowly; it fits the data only if nearly all the DNA differences between humans and chimpanzees are harmless ones, which is what the genome scientists also concluded.
Some of the old original papers could not be opened in the time allowed, so those rules are written from memory and need checking.

glossary.fixation: when a new gene version spreads until every individual in the population has it
glossary.fixation probability: the chance that a new gene version eventually reaches everyone
glossary.neutral mutation: a DNA change that neither helps nor harms its carrier
glossary.mutation rate (mu): how often a DNA letter is copied wrongly, per letter per generation
glossary.substitution rate (k): how fast DNA differences become permanent in a whole species
glossary.N and Ne (effective population size): the number of breeding individuals, adjusted so the maths of chance works as in an ideal population
glossary.selection coefficient (s): how much a gene version raises or lowers the number of offspring, as a fraction
glossary.dominance (h): how much of a gene version's effect shows when only one copy is carried
glossary.genetic drift: random change in how common a gene version is, caused by chance in who has offspring
glossary.Wright-Fisher model: a simple idealised population where each generation is a random draw from the previous one
glossary.diffusion limit: a maths shortcut that treats gene frequencies as changing smoothly in a large population
glossary.mutation-selection balance: the steady level of a harmful gene version, where new mistakes arrive as fast as selection removes them
glossary.mutational load: the drop in average fitness of a population caused by harmful mutations
glossary.Haldane's cost of selection: the number of deaths or failed births needed to replace one gene version by a better one, which limits how fast helpful changes can spread
glossary.drift barrier: the point where an improvement is so small that chance overwhelms selection, so it cannot be perfected further
glossary.nearly neutral theory: the idea that slightly harmful changes act as harmless in small populations
glossary.dN/dS: the rate of protein-changing DNA changes divided by the rate of silent ones
glossary.divergence (d): the fraction of DNA letters that differ between two species
glossary.generation time (g): the average age of parents when their offspring are born
glossary.pedigree or trio sequencing: reading the DNA of parents and child to count new mutations directly
glossary.ancestral polymorphism: differences that already existed in the ancestor population before two species split
glossary.molecular clock: using the steady build-up of DNA differences to date when species split
glossary.McDonald-Kreitman test: a method comparing differences within and between species to estimate how many changes were helpful
glossary.epistasis: when the effect of one gene change depends on other gene changes
glossary.DFE: distribution of fitness effects, the spread of how helpful or harmful new mutations are
glossary.TMRCA: time back to the most recent common ancestor of a set of gene copies
glossary.pi (nucleotide diversity): the average fraction of DNA letters that differ between two individuals of one species
